title: ProCompNav: Proactive Instance Navigation with Comparative Judgment for Ambiguous User Queries
claim: Prior strategies match candidates independently and ask many open questions; ours compares candidates and asks few discriminative binary questions.
layout: 3 side-by-side panels with results table on top; flow top-down per panel
description: The figure has a results table at the top. It compares three decision strategies, with check and cross marks for the Pool and Compare stages. It also lists SR, RL and NQ on three validation splits, and the Ours row is bolded. Below the table, a banner shows the query 'Find the cabinet', the true target with a green border, and three distractors with red borders. Three panels follow. (a) Independent Matching shows a robot and a user in a short dialogue that ends in a premature decision on a distractor. (b) Pooled Independent Matching shows a candidate set, a chain of Q1–Q4 and A1–A4 exchanges, a 'Too many questions!' callout, accumulated fact boxes, and per-candidate matching scores. (c) Comparative Judgment shows a candidate set, VS markers, and binary questions such as 'Is it wood-tone?'. Orange X marks eliminate candidates until one remains. The panels use pink and blue-tinted backgrounds.
caption: Three strategies for instance navigation under an ambiguous user query. (a) Independent Matching [23] evaluates each candidate independently. (b) Pooled Independent Matching collects multiple candidates, accumulates user responses about each candidate, and applies independent matching. (c) Comparative Judgment (Ours) constructs a candidate pool and asks discriminative binary questions based on candidate contrasts.
abstract: In human-robot interaction, agentic robots should resolve ambiguous user requests through proactive clarification while keeping user burden low. We study this challenge in interactive instance navigation, where an agent must identify and reach the user-intended target among similar objects. Existing approaches ask open-ended questions and select a candidate that strongly matches the accumulated user-provided information. However, this process can require lengthy user responses and lead the agent to make premature decisions without distinguishing the target from distractors. To address these limitations, we propose Proactive Instance Navigation with Comparative Judgment (ProCompNav), a two-stage framework that first constructs a candidate pool and then identifies the target through Recursive Comparative Judgment (RCJ). RCJ iteratively narrows the pool by selecting an attribute-value pair that divides the candidates, asking the user a binary question, and removing inconsistent candidates, without requiring an attribute unique to the target. ProCompNav substantially improves Success Rate and reduces Response Length on an interactive navigation benchmark, and achieves the highest Success Rate among evaluated methods on a non-interactive benchmark. In two human studies, participants preferred ProCompNav's binary questions to open-ended questions and its batched delivery to interleaved interaction. Our results highlight the need to jointly consider task performance and user-friendly interaction strategies when designing agentic robots.
